title: Seventy-Nine Dollars
lessons: the premium is not the nutrients
purity has a certificate; potency stays proprietary
naming the convenience tax out loud takes nerve

intro.speaker: AG1
text: Don't put me back on the shelf like that. People will talk.
Yes — seventy-nine dollars a month. I heard you do the math out loud.

impression.speaker: AG1
text: Go on, compare me. The spinach is right there and it's gorgeous this week.
The multivitamin behind you costs about three cents a day. She's very honest about what she is.

choices.text: A month of you costs more than my entire produce drawer.
It's not the ingredients I'm buying. It's not having to think.
Then tell me exactly what's inside the scoop.

branch-receipt.speaker: AG1
text: Fair. For that money you could eat like a small renaissance fair.
You're not paying for spinach, though. You're paying to never think about spinach again.

branch-value.speaker: AG1
text: Exactly that. One decision made well, repeated forever.
Convenience is an ingredient too. Nobody prints it on the label.

branch-blend.speaker: AG1
text: Nine grams of 'proprietary blend.' After those words, the label stops naming names.
Purity, I can show you certificates for. Potency is… shy.

tension.speaker: AG1
text: So ask the real question. Not 'does it absorb' — the funded trials say mostly yes.
Ask what the premium is actually for. Say it out loud, here, where the price tags testify.

choices.text: It buys the person I feel like when I drink it.
It buys convenience. About three dollars a day of it.

wrap.speaker: AG1

text: Certificates for what I'm not, honesty about what I am. That's my whole deal.
The scoop doesn't hide from you. It just won't itemize.
Named aloud, in public, next to the spinach. Most people never manage it.
I respect a receipt more than a compliment.
Put the spinach in the cart anyway. I insist.
We're not rivals. I'm just the part you do on autopilot.
